newsitem.title: UK: Cocoa seen heading for supply deficit again.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa seen heading for supply deficit again.

text.p: As cocoa nations met on Thursday for a fourth day of talks in London on output cuts, crop forecasters are projecting a return to a world cocoa supply deficit in 1996/97 after a year of excess production.
Analysts said although the forecasts varied significantly, the supply shortfall could be sizeable and could surpass the 34-year-high of 200,000 tonnes in 1994/95.
Strong global demand for chocolates, cocoa's main product, is expected to fuel cocoa consumption which is expected to outpace production.
"The cocoa market is undergoing a structural change towards the deficit," an economist at a U.K. research house said. "Last year's surplus seems to be an exception rather than the rule."
"We are seeing an expansion in chocolate consumption in South America and in other fast-growing economies," he said.
A wide supply gap could help stimulate flagging prices and boost farmers' income, analysts said.
One analyst forecast prices to rise by 60 percent to 1,600 pounds (US$2,487) a tonne, from 1,000 pounds now, within the next six to 12 months.
"We estimate that grindings (of cocoa beans) will increase by six percent this season, the highest growth rate since 1988/89," British commodity house ED & F Man said.
"Chocolate consumption growth has been strong in 1996, even in the more mature markets of Western Europe and North America," it said in its latest cocoa crop report.

The crop forecasts from British and U.S. trade and research houses coincided with a meeting in London of the International Cocoa Organisation (ICCO), which groups leading cocoa producer and consumer states.

The meeting is aimed at reviewing the ICCO plan to slash world output by 375,000 tonnes over five years from 1994. The 375,000-tonne reduction was seen needed at that time to balance world supply with demand and ensure more renumerative prices to farmers.

No decision was taken yet on whether the ICCO would keep to its annual target of a 75,000-tonne cutback for 1996/97 but published ICCO supply forecasts showed a 225,000-deficit for the coming crop without even trimming a single tonne.
The British trade house Man projected a world cocoa surplus of 36,000 tonnes in the current 1995/96 (Oct/Sept) season, up from its May forecast of a 2,000-tonne surplus.
Man saw total output from top grower Ivory Coast at a record of 1.125 million tonnes, up from its previous forecast of 1.10 million and against 1994/95's harvest of 876,000.
The ICCO on Wednesday said the Ivorian crop could fall to 950,000 tonnes in 1996/97.
The last time cocoa was in deficit was in 1994/95, when it recorded a gap of 200,000 tonnes.
There was market talk earlier in the week that Man could report a supply shortfall of between 150,000 and 180,000 tonnes for the coming season.
Man forecast the total 1995/96 world net cocoa harvest at a record 2.732 million tonnes against 1994/95's 2.344 million.
Total world grindings (consumption) were seen at 2.697 million tonnes against 2.544 million in 1994/95.
